nameStory: The 'monkeyflower' name comes from the flower's face-like appearance - if you look closely at the bloom, the upper and lower lips create what looks like a grinning monkey face! The 'Allegheny' part refers to the Allegheny Mountains, part of this wildflower's native eastern range.
description: Allegheny monkeyflower is a cheerful wetland wildflower that brightens up marshy areas with its snapdragon-like blooms. This native perennial can grow anywhere from about 8 inches to over 3 feet tall, sending up sturdy square stems from underground runners. The tubular flowers come in shades of lavender, blue, pink, or red and have a distinctive two-lipped shape that really does look like a little face.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tubular blooms 1-3 inches long with two lips - a smaller upper lip and a larger, puffy lower lip that often has darker spots or lines. Colors range from lavender and blue to pink and red.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped to oblong leaves up to 3 inches long that clasp directly onto the stem without stalks. They're arranged in opposite pairs and feel smooth and hairless.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Spreads by underground runners (rhizomes) to form colonies in wet areas. Stems stand upright and feel distinctly square when you roll them between your fingers.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops small capsules enclosed within the ribbed, tube-like calyx that remains after the flower petals fall away.

habitat: Look for Allegheny monkeyflower in consistently wet or boggy areas throughout New England - along stream banks, pond edges, marshes, wet meadows, and roadside ditches. It thrives in full sun to partial shade and can handle seasonal flooding. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other moisture-loving plants.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground runners as the weather warms. Fresh green foliage begins growing up the square stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from June through August, when the monkey-faced flowers are most abundant and colorful. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may continue into early fall, followed by seed capsule development. Foliage begins to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground rhizomes. Only dead stems may remain visible above ground in protected areas.

funFact: Monkeyflowers are pollinated by bumblebees that have to be strong enough to pry open the flower's 'mouth' - the lower lip acts like a landing platform, but the bee has to push past the upper lip to reach the nectar, getting dusted with pollen in the process!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with garden snapdragons, but those are much larger, more densely flowered, and found in cultivated areas rather than wetlands. Wild bergamot has a similar flower shape but grows in dry areas and has a minty smell when crushed.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'monkeyflower,' this plant was recently moved from the snapdragon family (Scrophulariaceae) to the lopseed family (Phrymaceae) based on genetic studies - botanists are still updating field guides to reflect this change!
compareHints: Allegheny monkeyflower can be distinguished from its close relative, sharpwing monkeyflower, by its stalkless leaves that clasp the stem directly. Sharpwing monkeyflower has leaves on distinct stalks (petioles) and has winged ridges running down its stem, while Allegheny's stem is square but not winged.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to Allegheny monkeyflower, sharpwing monkeyflower has much more pronounced winged ridges on its stems that feel distinctly sharp when you run your finger along them.
